text: Gland [Lat. glans , an acorn]: Ger. Drüse ; Fr. glande ; Ital. glandula . A secreting organ or part; an agglomeration of grandular epithelial cells, arranged in a great variety of ways, viz. in tubes -- tubular glands, simple and compound; in sacs -- 'acinous,' 'racemose,' or 'saccular,' simple and compound; ductless glands. Cf. INTERNAL SECRETION. Originally applied to oval bodies on the course of the lymphatics, and these are still referred to under the name 'lymphatic glands' (Quain, &c.). The tendency, however, is to restrict the term to collections of true secreting cells. As to 'lymph-glands. -- It is a misnomer to call these structures glands, for they produce no secretion. A better term is lymph-nodes.' Cf. Dunham, Histology (1898), 114. See LYMPH. ( C.F.H. )
